blocks.text: An iroko tree can lift water more than thirty metres from its roots to its topmost leaves, with no heart, no pump and no moving parts. The engine that does it is simply water evaporating from the leaves.

blocks.markdown:
## Why plants need a transport system

A plant makes its food in the leaves but absorbs water and mineral salts through the roots. The two must therefore travel in opposite directions, sometimes over many metres. Small plants such as mosses can rely on diffusion alone, but any plant more than a few centimetres tall needs specialised **vascular tissue**.

There are two vascular tissues, and every examination question on this topic rests on telling them apart.

blocks.caption: Xylem carries water up; phloem carries food in both directions

blocks.title: How to picture the arrangement
blocks.text: In a young dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles form a ring near the outside, with xylem on the inner side of each bundle and phloem on the outer side, separated by cambium. In a root the xylem sits in the very centre, often as a star shape, with phloem between its arms. In a leaf the vascular bundle forms the midrib and veins, again with xylem above and phloem below.

blocks.markdown:
## The path of water from soil to air

Water takes one continuous journey. Learn it as an ordered list, because WAEC frequently asks you to "trace the path".

1. Soil water is absorbed through the **root hairs** by osmosis, because the cell sap of the root hair is more concentrated than the soil solution.
2. Water passes from cell to cell across the root cortex by osmosis, down a water potential gradient.
3. It enters the **xylem** vessels in the centre of the root.
4. It is pulled up the xylem of the root, stem and leaf as a continuous column.
5. In the leaf it moves into the **mesophyll** cells and wets their surfaces.
6. It evaporates into the air spaces of the leaf.
7. It diffuses out through the **stomata** as water vapour. This loss is **transpiration**.

blocks.title: Three terms that are easily confused
blocks.text: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mostly through stomata. Transpiration pull is the suction force created in the xylem as that water is lost. Guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets from leaf margins, which happens at night when transpiration is low and root pressure is high.

blocks.markdown:
### What actually lifts the water

Three forces act together, and the cohesion–tension explanation combines them:

- **Transpiration pull.** Evaporation from the mesophyll leaves those cells short of water, so they draw water from the xylem, putting the whole column under tension.
- **Cohesion and adhesion.** Water molecules attract one another (cohesion), so the column does not break, and they cling to the lignified xylem walls (adhesion), so it does not slip back.
- **Root pressure.** Osmosis into the root pushes water a short way up from below. This is a minor contribution and cannot by itself reach the top of a tall tree.

Capillarity in the narrow vessels also helps, but transpiration pull is by far the largest force.

## Factors affecting the rate of transpiration

Anything that speeds up evaporation from the leaf, or steepens the water vapour gradient between the leaf and the air, increases transpiration.

rows: Water molecules gain kinetic energy and evaporate faster
The air already holds much vapour, so the diffusion gradient out of the leaf is small
Moist air is blown away from the leaf surface, keeping the gradient steep
Light opens the stomata, so more vapour escapes
More stomata and more surface from which to evaporate
Thick waxy cuticle or sunken stomata
Water loss through the epidermis is reduced, an adaptation of desert plants
Stomata close to conserve water, so vapour cannot escape
blocks.caption: Light, temperature, humidity and wind are the four factors most often examined

blocks.title: Reading a potometer experiment
blocks.prompt: A leafy shoot is fitted into a potometer. In still air at 28 °C the air bubble moves 12 mm in 5 minutes. A fan is then switched on and the bubble moves 30 mm in the next 5 minutes. Explain the result and state one precaution needed for a fair comparison.

steps.text: A potometer measures the rate at which the shoot takes up water, and this uptake is assumed to equal the rate of transpiration.
In still air the rate is 12 mm ÷ 5 min, that is 2.4 mm per minute.
With the fan on the rate is 30 mm ÷ 5 min, that is 6.0 mm per minute, two and a half times faster.
The fan blows away the layer of moist air that normally collects just outside the stomata. This keeps the concentration of water vapour outside the leaf low.
The diffusion gradient from the leaf air spaces to the outside air therefore stays steep, so water vapour diffuses out faster and the shoot draws up more water.
Precaution: keep temperature, light intensity and humidity the same in both runs, and use the same shoot with the same leaf area, so that only air movement changes.

blocks.answer: Air movement increased the transpiration rate from 2.4 to 6.0 mm per minute by removing saturated air from the leaf surface and maintaining a steep diffusion gradient. All other factors must be kept constant for a fair test.

items: Transpiration is useful: it cools the leaf, pulls up water and carries dissolved mineral salts to the leaves.
Transpiration is also a risk: excessive loss causes wilting, and prolonged wilting kills the plant.
A plant loses over ninety per cent of the water it absorbs by transpiration; only a small fraction is used in photosynthesis.
Wilting happens when water is lost faster than it is absorbed, so the cells lose turgor and the leaves and soft stems droop.
Desert plants reduce loss with thick cuticles, sunken stomata, few stomata, rolled leaves, spines instead of leaves and fleshy water-storing stems.

blocks.title: Do not say xylem is alive
blocks.text: Mature xylem vessels are dead and empty, which is exactly what makes them good pipes. Phloem sieve tubes are living. A common error is to claim phloem carries water and xylem carries food, so fix the direction in your mind: xylem goes up with water, phloem goes both ways with food.

points: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards in dead lignified vessels; phloem translocates dissolved food in both directions in living sieve tubes.
Water is absorbed by osmosis through root hairs, crosses the cortex, enters the xylem, rises to the leaf and evaporates through the stomata as transpiration.
Transpiration pull, helped by cohesion and adhesion of water and by root pressure, lifts the water column without any pump.
High temperature, bright light, wind and low humidity all increase the rate of transpiration.
Transpiration cools the plant and moves mineral salts, but excessive loss leads to wilting.
